Neonatal Copper sharks (Carcharhinus brachyurus) emerge from their mothers as well-developed pups, with their total length at birth typically measuring 65 cm [Lb = 65 cm], though a range of 59 to 70 cm has been documented across different populations. This birth size places them among the larger elasmobranch neonates relative to maternal dimensions. Gestation is prolonged, lasting approximately 730 days [ab = approximately 730 days] under the thermal regime these sharks typically experience, which hovers around 17.4 °C [T = 17.4 °C]. The extended intrauterine development is characteristic of many carcharhinid sharks that exhibit placental viviparity, allowing the embryos to reach a considerable size before parturition. Observations from both field studies and captive environments suggest that the gestation period can vary with maternal nutritional condition and water temperature, but the two-year cycle appears to be a stable feature of the species' reproductive biology. Following parturition, the neonates are immediately independent and must forage for themselves, a challenge reflected in relatively high early mortality rates among young-of-the-year individuals inhabiting coastal nursery grounds.

The maximum recorded body mass for adult Copper sharks is based on a well-established length-weight relationship, with the ultimate wet weight reaching approximately 208,700 grams [Wwi = approximately 208,700 grams]. This substantial mass is attained only after many years of growth, reflecting the species' high trophic position as an apex predator in temperate coastal ecosystems. Females grow to a considerably larger ultimate total length than males, reaching up to 325 cm [Li = up to 325 cm], whereas males rarely exceed 300 cm [Li = 300 cm]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in maximum size is common among requiem sharks and is thought to be linked to the energetic demands of gestation and parturition in females. The length-weight conversion reveals a robust build, with large adult females often weighing over 200 kilograms, making C. brachyurus one of the heavier members of its genus in temperate waters. Such body sizes are typically encountered in offshore environments where prey availability is highest.

The onset of sexual maturation in Copper sharks occurs at different lengths for each sex, with females reaching puberty at around 175 cm [Lp = around 175 cm] total length, although a broader range of 160 to 190 cm has been reported in some regional studies. Males mature slightly smaller, beginning their reproductive life at approximately 170 cm [Lp = approximately 170 cm] total length, with reported variation from 160 to 180 cm. This size at puberty corresponds to a significant portion of the species' ultimate length, indicating a life-history strategy that prioritizes somatic growth before investing in reproduction. The age at which these lengths are achieved is not precisely known for all populations, but growth-ring analyses from vertebrae suggest that females may require a decade or more to reach pubertal size in the cooler parts of their range. The discrepancy between the sexes in pubertal size aligns with the general pattern observed in elasmobranchs, where females delay maturity to accommodate the physical demands of bearing large litters.

At the water temperatures typical of their subtropical and warm-temperate habitats, Copper sharks exhibit a slow, K-selected life-history strategy. The species produces litters ranging from 7 to 20 pups [N_R_i = litters ranging from 7 to 20 pups], and the reproductive frequency is approximately one litter every two years [F_R_i = approximately one litter every two years], constrained by the lengthy gestation period. This biennial cycle unfolds under ambient conditions of 17.4 °C [T = 17.4 °C]. This low fecundity relative to teleost fishes makes the species highly susceptible to overfishing, as population recovery from depletion is inherently slow. The trade-off between producing relatively few, large offspring and the high maternal investment per pup is a defining feature of the genus Carcharhinus.

Longevity is another key aspect of the Copper shark's life cycle, with the maximum lifespan estimated at 30 years [am = 30 years] under the thermal conditions of 17.4 °C [T = 17.4 °C]. This extended lifespan allows for multiple reproductive events over an individual's lifetime, partially compensating for the low annual fecundity. Field studies using tag-recapture data and vertebral ageing have confirmed individuals exceeding twenty-five years of age in wild populations. The species' long life and late maturity mean that a significant portion of the population consists of large, reproductively valuable adults. Senescence in large sharks is poorly understood, but the onset of age-related declines in physiological performance appears gradual. From a conservation perspective, the combination of delayed puberty, low reproductive output, and substantial longevity places C. brachyurus among the most vulnerable coastal shark species to targeted and bycatch fisheries across its global distribution.
